To evaluate the risks of DDIs clinically, a systematic review of the literature and clinical studies are conducted to assess the magnitude of interaction, the population at risk, and the potential consequences (Huang et al., 2017). The interaction risk is evaluated using various tools, such as the Drug Interaction Probability Scale (DIPS) and the Clinical Interaction Scale (CIS), which take into account the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties of the interacting drugs (Lehmann et al., 2018). Additionally, in vitro studies using human liver microsomes and recombinant CYP enzymes are used to predict the potential for DDIs (Obach, 1999). Furthermore, pharmacokinetic modeling and simulation can also be employed to estimate the impact of DDIs on drug concentrations and efficacy (Wang et al., 2015).

Theoretical modeling has also been used to understand the impact of minimum wage policies on employment outcomes. This approach involves the use of economic theory to model the behavior of firms and workers in response to minimum wage policies (Burgess and Redmond, 2006).
